title: Federal Prosecutors Decline to Bring Civil Rights Charges Against ICE Agent Castro
excerpt: Federal prosecutors in Minneapolis considered but ultimately declined to charge ICE agent Christian Castro with federal civil rights violations for the January shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis — the same day the third witness to the Houston ICE shooting was released from custody.
content:
On August 30, 2026, MPR News reported that federal prosecutors in Minneapolis had considered but ultimately declined to charge ICE Agent Christian Castro with civil rights violations under federal law for the January 14, 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

The decision means Castro faces only state-level charges in Minnesota — charges that have so far proven unenforceable due to Texas Governor Abbott's refusal to extradite and Castro's release from Texas custody on August 27. The federal non-prosecution decision was made even as the DOJ had acknowledged that its civil rights division held conversations with local Minnesota prosecutors.

  • Castro had been charged by Hennepin County prosecutors with four felony counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.
  • Federal charges would have been brought under 18 U.S.C. § 242, which criminalizes deprivation of rights under color of law — a statute the DOJ declined to apply despite video evidence contradicting Castro's account of events.
  • The federal declination came after earlier reports indicated the Justice Department was actively considering such charges.

The combination of the extradition failure and the federal non-prosecution decision left Castro facing no immediate legal consequence, illustrating a structural gap in accountability for federal law enforcement agents who commit misconduct across state lines.
